title: Investigation on strain localization and hardening of dual-phase steel by hetero-deformation induced stress
abstract: Strain hardening remains challenging for maintaining the plasticity of metals, especially those of high strength. The hetero-deformation induced (HDI) stress can effectively alleviate the problem, specifically with a large mechanical response mismatch. Accordingly, the strain localization and hardening in dual-phase steel consisting of ductile ferrite (F) and almost undeformed bainite (B) were investigated by calculating HDI stress (σh) based on the tensile load-unload-reload (LUR) hysteresis loop and modified equation. Of particular note is that strain localization first appears in the ferrite, and then transfers to the F/B interface during tensile LUR. The generated σh by the accumulation of geometrically necessary dislocations (GNDs) inhibits the mobile dislocation, thereby reducing the strain difference, which promotes the transfer of strain localization. The transformation of strain localization changes the hardening behavior from ferrite hardening to F/B interfacial hardening. The results state clearly that the σh enhances strain hardening while induced strain localization maintains tensile plasticity. Eventually, with the increase σh, the failure of dual-phase steel tends to transition from initial ductile fracture to brittle fracture.
journal: Journal of Materials Research and Technology

sections.heading: Introduction
paragraphs: The combination of favorable strength and plasticity is an attractive prospect for the application of metallic materials [ 1 , 2 ]. However, when the yield strength increases significantly, the plasticity becomes disappointingly low [ 3 ]. This is mainly due to the deficiency of strain hardening in cold working, which almost makes the traditional dislocation motion fail to coordinate the tensile plasticity [ 4 , 5 ]. Currently, there exist two distinct strategies that have been successfully implemented to effectively coordinate the intricate relationship between tensile plasticity and strength. The first method is to promote the storage of dislocations to restore intragranular dislocation motion for strain hardening, for instance, nanoprecipitation [ 6 ] and grain refinement [ 7 ]. Moving on to the next point, the contributions of intergranular hetero-deformation induced (HDI) stress [ 8 ] and strain localization [ 9 ] to tensile plasticity and strength in different various types of  trans -scale heterostructures are introduced.

The heterogeneous structure of metallic materials has garnered significant attention in recent years, captivating the interest of many [ 10–12 ]. The heterostructure is usually characterized by a cross-scale microstructure of grain size, including heterogeneous grain structure in single-phase structure [ 10 ], dual-phase [ 11 ], or multi-phase microstructure [ 12 ]. During the loading process, it is inevitably a large mismatch in the plastic response, such as yield strength and flow stress [ 13 ]. For example, strong nano-sized grains of almost no ductility in metallic materials, which is in sharp contrast to the large ductile soft coarse particles [ 14 ]. This appearance starts from many dual-phase alloys from the plastic deformation incompatibility between the hard phases and the soft matrix [ 15 ]. These soft matrix phases exhibit a high degree of strain localization, which is caused by geometrically necessary dislocations (GNDs) required to accommodate the local mismatch in the tensile plasticity of the soft matrix phase [ 16 , 17 ]. Additionally, these GNDs accumulate and interact with various boundaries, triggering the intergranular HDI stress, which plays a key role in strain hardening [ 9 , 18 ].

The dual-phase and multi-phase are representatives of heterostructures [ 11 , 12 ]. During the straining process, the micro heterogeneous deformation necessarily occurs at the phase/grain boundary, which is still due to the large mechanical mismatch among varying phases [ 19 ]. HDI strengthening between different phases has been evidenced to ameliorate plasticity in strain hardening [ 20 ]. Further, Liu et al. [ 21 ] confirmed that the hardening behavior induced by high HDI stress through GNDs is the main reason for the excellent combination of strength and ductility of heterostructures. In addition, Chou et al. [ 22 ] revealed by a modified load-unload-reload (LUR) tensile testing that high HDI stress can lead to the yield stress of the grains strengthened by the dislocations pileups against the interface being effectively increased. On the whole, to obtain the excellent combination of plasticity and strength, the research on the hetero-deformation of dual-phase structures mainly focuses on HDI stress induced hardening behavior.

Inspired by this, the hetero-deformation was investigated in detail during tensile LUR deformation in dual-phase steel. The ductile ferrite was the matrix, while almost undeformed bainite was the hard phase. The steel has a large mechanical mismatch between the two phases, which makes it an ideal heterostructure to reveal the key role of strain localization and hardening induced by HDI stress. This facilitates further designing the relationship between the tensile strength and plasticity of dual-phase steel.

sections.heading: Experimental material
paragraphs: In this work, commercial pipeline steel (X80 dual-phase steel) with a composition of 0.045 C, 0.19 Si, 0.012 P, 0.0023 S, 1.64 Mn, 0.23 Cr, 0.006 Ni, 0.088 Nb, 0.005 V, 0.011 Ti, 0.0097 Cu, 0.033Al, 0.0003 B and the balance being Fe (all in wt.%) was used. The received test material was annealed at 773 K for 2 h for removing residual stress.

sections.heading: Tensile LUR test and tensile behavior
paragraphs:
For the sake of better evaluating the HDI stress hardening of the tensile LUR, the tensile LUR test was carried out on the WAW-600C servo universal tester at a quasi-static strain rate, and the displacement control and force control were used to measure. The tensile rate was  V 
                         
                            1 
                          = 2 mm/min, the tensile LUR strain was 1–5%, and the design strain amount is increased by 1% each time. Tensile specimens were cut from the annealed plate with the longitudinal axis parallel to the rolling direction. The cross-section area was 40 mm × 18.4 mm and the length was 200 mm. The extensometer was attached to measure the tensile strain during the tensile deformation. Three tensile specimens were prepared under the same tensile condition for three times of tensile tests to avoid experimental errors. To analyze hetero-deformation capacity after HDI stress strengthen, the rod-shaped tensile sample was cut in the uniform deformation zone of the sample after the LUR test. The round bar sample was subjected to a tensile fracture test on the HT-2402 computer servo-controlled material testing machine, and the displacement control and force control were used to measure, the tensile rate was  V 
                         
                            2 
                          = 0.5 mm/min. In the same condition, three round bar specimens were used for three tensile fracture tests. In this paper, the appendix shows the detailed dimensions of the two tensile test specimens.

sections.heading: Morphology and dislocation
paragraphs:
Metallographic observation of dual-phase ( Fig. 1 
                         (a)) was implemented by an optical microscope (OM, AXIO SCOPE-A1) after grinding, polishing, and then etched by 4% nital solution (nitric acid in ethanol) for 15 s. It indicated that the microstructure consists of ductile ferrite (F) and non-deformable bainite (B) [ 23 ]. The calculated volume fraction of about 27.3% of granular bainite was mainly distributed along the grain boundary of ferrite, and a large number of small bainite islands are distributed in the ferrite matrix. Meanwhile, the tensile fracture morphology of the dual-phase steel after cutting and acetone cleaning was analyzed by scanning electron microscopy (SEM Hitachi-S4800). The microstructure evolution of ferrite and bainite in a dual-phase heterostructure with different tensile LUR was investigated by electron backscatter diffraction (EBSD, THERMO QUASOR). The test samples were extracted along the cross-sectional direction, and parallel to the loading axis. The samples for EBSD were ground, mechanically polished, and then electrolytically polished (performed using a step size of 150 nm and an accelerating voltage of 20 kV). The dislocation morphology and configuration during the tensile LUR test were observed by Transmission electron microscope (TEM, JEM-200CX). The samples for TEM were mechanically ground to produce thin plates of 50 μm thickness and 3 mm diameter, and then twin-jet electro-polished in a mixed solution of 5% perchloric acid and 95% ethanol. The controlling parameters were: a voltage of 35 V, a current of 40 mA, and a temperature of −30  
                            ◦ 
                         
                         C . The TEM foils were observed using a field-emission transmission electron microscope at the bright field with 200 kV acceleration voltage.

The total dislocation density of the F/B dual-phase heterostructure was determined by micro-beam X-ray diffraction (XRD, D8 DISCOVER A25). Micro-beam XRD scanning was carried out in the 2θ range of 40–110° ( Fig. 1 (b)), and then the step was defined as 0.02°, and the retention time was defined as 0.4 s [ 24 ]. The modified Williamson-Hall method was used to calculate the total dislocation density after tensile LUR [ 24 , 25 ]. It was well known that the XRD peak spectrum was the result of the instrument and the sample under test, so the contribution of the instrument to the peak broadening had been subtracted from the raw data before the dislocation density was calculated.

sections.heading: Measurement of hetero-deformation induced ( HDI ) stress
paragraphs:
To investigate the origin of the strain localization and hardening of dual-phase steel heterostructure and the contribution of HDI stress to high yield strength. We carried out tensile LUR ( Fig. 2 
                         (a)) to study the Bauschinger effect, from which we can estimate the contribution of the HDI stress and dislocation hardening to flow stress [ 26 ]. As shown in  Fig. 2 (b), the hysteresis loop appears in the LUR process, which is effective proof of the existence of HDI stress and also the basis for calculating HDI stress.  Fig. 2 (c) displays a schematic diagram of the hysteresis loop during tensile LUR, in which the OAB curve represents the tensile stage, the BCDE curve represents the unloading stage, and the EFG curve represents the re-tensile stage. When tensile to point B of the true-stress/true-strain curve, the sample is unloaded, the flow stress during unloading is σ 0 , and the unloading strain is ε 0 . The BC segment of the unloading curve is a quasi-elastic stage, which is related to the stress relaxation or viscoelasticity of the material [ 27 ]. The stress drop in this stage is called the thermal component of the flow stress (σ∗), and the value is approximate to the yield stress of the loading curve. The unloading curve CD is the linear elastic stage, the unloading elastic modulus is recorded as E u , point D is the unloading yield point, and the unloading yield stress is σ 
                            u 
                         , which is formed by the reverse slip of the movable dislocation driven by the HDI stress. The reloading curve EF is the linear elastic stage during reloading, and its elastic modulus is recorded as E r . Point F is the reloading yield point, and the yield stress is σ r . Yang [ 28 ] presented a modified formula for calculating HDI stress from an unloading true stress-strain curve in  Fig. 2 (c).

The calculated σ h  values are displayed in  Fig. 2 (d), and the σ h  increases from 235 MPa to 360 MPa with increased tensile LUR. sections.heading: Strain localization and dislocation density of dual-phase steel
paragraphs:
Fig. 4 
                         (a) emerges the inverse pole figure in the Z direction for 3% tensile LUR [ 29 ]. The band slope (BS) values are more sensitive to crystal lattice distortion, which can discuss the strain localization induced by σ h  [ 30 ]. The higher the BS value, the much greater degree of strain localization in ferrite and they become the darker areas in  Fig. 4 (b). According to statistical analysis of the specific BS values of ferrite and bainite, the distribution map of BS values can be acquired from  Fig. 4 (c). The symmetrical peaks of BS values of bainite and ferrite phases are obtained by Gaussian curve fitting. As can be seen in  Fig. 4 (d), the ferrite peak gradually shifts to the bainite peak, while the bainite peak increases slightly, which means that the ferrite has a larger strain localization [ 17 ]. With the increase of tensile LUR, the strain localization difference between ferrite and bainite is reduced, which is easy to induce interface deformation [ 31 ]. It indicates that the strain localization first occurs in ferrite, and with the increase of σ h , the strain localization lies at the interface of ferrite and bainite, adapting to heterostructure deformation incompatibility.

Kernell average misorientation (KAM) gives a piece of detailed information on the evolution of strain localization in the microstructure [ 32 ]. The KAM quantifies the average misorientation around a measurement point concerning a defined set of nearest or nearest plus second-nearest neighbor points. In our paper, KAM is calculated for a maximum of 5° of misorientation considering the first neighbor. Representative KAM maps of dual-phase steels are shown in  Fig. 5 
                         (a and b), at 1–3% tensile LUR, the strain localization is higher within the ferritic matrix, while the strain localization near the F/B interface is lower. The KAM map in  Fig. 5 (b and c) also exhibits similar behavior for ferrite grains, where the F/B interface has high strain localization during 3–5% tensile LUR. In ferrite, GNDs are considered the main reason for enhancing strain localization, and the KAM method is generally used to calculate the GNDs density [ 33 ]. The averaged KAM values can be defined as a measure for the local misorientations and are related to the GNDs density (ρ GNDs ) as follow in Eq  (2)  [ 34 ]:

                         where σ is true stress, ε is true strain, K is strength coefficient, and  n  is strain hardening exponent, which is a measure of deformation resistance [ 36 ].

After tensile LUR deformation, it can be seen from the tensile true stress-strain curve that the true stress of the dual-phase steel increases, and the fracture point gradually moves backward, indicating that the strain hardening ability gradually decreases ( Fig. 6 
                         (a)). It should be noted that the  n  exhibits two different strain hardening rates (Stage I and Ⅱ). After 1–3% tensile LUR, the strain hardening shows a significant downward trend with σ h  increases (Stage I), while the downward trend is tardily (Stage Ⅱ) after 3–5% tensile LUR ( Fig. 6 (b)). In the tensile plasticity process, the dislocations in the ferrite are first activated and begin to slip along the slip plane [ 32 ]. The σ h  induced by the GNDs makes the  n  decrease observably, resulting in the gradual hardening of ferrite. Subsequently, the difference between soft ferrite hardening and hard bainite strain decreases, strain localization gradually transfers to the interface, which leads to interface hardening [ 37 ]. The transfer of strain localization and hardening in dual-phase steels results in two degrees of improvement in tensile strength and plasticity. On the whole, the yield strength and tensile strength of the material are significantly further improved after the tensile fracture, while the elongation (stage Ⅰ) and shrinkage are slightly reduced ( Fig. 6 (c and d)). The interface of ferrite and bainite is gradually hardened, which is conducive to the tensile deformation of dual-phase steel during tensile fracture [ 38 ]. In short, the HDI strengthening enhances the strength, while the σ h  induces strain localization and hardening, which helps to retain the tensile plasticity of dual-phase steel.

sections.heading: Ductile-brittle transition of tensile fracture
paragraphs:
In the early stage of LUR deformation, the existing hard particles or inclusions in dual-phase steels will serve as nucleation sites for the formation of microvoids in the ferrite tend to grow, resulting in severe internal tearing of the ferrite, forming a dimple shape ( Fig. 7 
                         (a and b)) [ 39 ]. After fracture morphology of 3% tensile LUR ( Fig. 7 (c)), the size of the dimples becomes significantly larger and depth becomes shallower, even the river pattern morphology appears. With increasing levels of LUR straining, the micropore nucleation appears at the interfaces, microcracks are formed at the interface and expanded along the phase boundaries, and the material appears to have brittle fracture morphology characteristics [ 40 ]. During this process, obvious dissociation cracks appear, forming a micro-brittle quasi-cleavage fracture morphology, which is in the shape of a river ( Fig. 7 (d)) [ 41 ]. In this paper, the mechanism of fracture morphology evolution from dimple shape to quasi-dissociated river pattern under tensile LUR deformation is closely related to HDI stress induced strain localization and hardening observed in dual-phase steel.

Furthermore, it is found from  Fig. 8 
                         (a–f) that the main crack propagation angle of the macroscopic fracture of the dual-phase steel gradually increases with the increased tensile LUR. For the undeformed specimen, the crack propagates along the direction of 45° to the tension axis, which is a typical shear fracture [ 42 ]. The fracture is uneven and has many twists and turns, which is a typical ripple pattern or serpentine slip pattern, and extends to both sides, and the expansion angle with the tension axis gradually increases from  Fig. 8 (a, g). When the tensile LUR strain increases to 3%, strain localization appear at the interface and cracks thus crack initiation at the interface and propagation along grain boundaries [ 43 ]. It can be seen from the tensile fracture that the crack propagation path near both sides of the fracture of the specimen is tortuous, and most of the fractures in the middle are relatively flat ( Fig. 8 (d, h)). Especially after the tensile LUR strain is 5%, the crack propagation angle (θ) is measured to be 85°, and the crack propagation path is almost perpendicular to the tensile direction  Fig. 8 (f, i). The stress state of the specimen is shown in  Fig. 8 (j), shear stress (τ) is the driving force of dislocation slip, normal stress (σ) affects the crack propagation path and process, and tensile stress (σ 0 ) affects the entire plastic strain and cracks propagation [ 41 ]. That is, when the local deformation of the specimen reaches the maximum shear strength, shear fracture occurs, the σ h  increases to suppress the  τ , and normal fracture occurs when the maximum normal fracture strength is reached [ 44 ]. Under the action of σ 0 , two different stress states are formed on the fracture surface with angle θ 0 , namely, the σ perpendicular to the fracture surface and the τ parallel to the fracture surface. Two stress states affect the crack propagation and dislocation slip respectively [ 42 ]. When considering the effect of the stress state on the fracture path of the crack, the σ and the τ can be expressed by the following formulas Eqs.  (4–5)  [ 45 ]:

sections.heading: Discussion
paragraphs:
During 1–3% tensile LUR strain, strain localization appears to have uneven scattered distribution in ferrite (Stage Ⅰ), and the GNDs density increases gradually ( Fig. 5 (d)). The reason is that the σ h  inhibits the mobile dislocation in ferrite, and thus the GNDs density increases markedly [ 15 ]. When the ferrite undergoes tensile plasticity, the dislocation source is activated first and the mobile dislocation starts to move along the slip plane ( Fig. 9 
                      (a, e)) [ 30 ]. However, the direction of σ h  is opposite to the direction of dislocation motion, with many GNDs being forced to accumulate in front of some obstacles in deformation, leading to strain hardening of ferrite. Simultaneously, the dislocation keeps moving and interacts in the same direction during the tensile LUR. The subsistent mobile dislocation in the previous strain path continues to slide in the same direction, which would increase the degree of dislocation tangles ( Fig. 9 (b)) [ 46 ]. Nevertheless, due to the limited number of dislocations, the dislocation dissolution rate is slower than the dislocation tangles rate, and the entanglement accumulates with the continuation of tensile LUR, substantial GNDs are formed under the inhibition of σ h  ( Fig. 9 (b and c)). In the ferrite, dislocation walls and cells can also develop during tensile LUR strain ( Fig. 9 (f)). Long-range back stress may develop inside the dislocation cells and forward stress may develop in the cell walls, which produce HDI strain hardening ( Fig. 9 (g)) [ 47 ]. As a result, the GNDs density in ferrite increases significantly and the degree of ferrite hardening is enhanced during 1–3% LUR tensile strain.

When tensile LUR strain is 3–5%, the density of GNDs increases, and the strain localization at the interface has appeared ( Fig. 5 (b–d)) and ( Fig. 9 (c and d)), which promotes the interface deformation of ferrite and bainite (Stage Ⅱ). At the same time, the σ h  accelerates the activation of dislocation sources near the interface, which promotes the accumulation and entanglement of dislocations on different slip planes, which may lead to multiple slips [ 48 ]. Multiple slips facilitated the intersection of dislocations on slip planes, thus increasing the probability of GNDs formation near the interface [ 49 ]. The GNDs density further increases and multiple slips create more dislocation connections and pile up, which form dislocation walls and cells ( Fig. 9 (d, f)) [ 38 ]. The appearance of the dislocation walls and cells enhances the dislocation storage and subsequent hardening of ferrite, which can reduce the plastic deformation difference between ferrite and bainite [ 50 ]. This noteworthy GNDs change makes ferrite hardening and promotes strain localization at the interface. Under the influence of σ h , the dislocation motion barrier increases accordingly and the interface hardening gradually occurs.

After yielding, the dislocation source inside the ferrite is activated first and begins to slip, resulting in plastic strain, while the bainite with higher yield strength continues to remain elastic, resulting in the incompatibility of deformation between the two phases [ 51 ]. To maintain the coordination of deformation at different grains, a large number of GNDs are formed near grain boundaries to avoid possible gaps or overlaps between grains [ 49 ]. These high-density GNDs tend to be in an orderly and regular arrangement at the grain boundaries, thus forming σ h  opposite to the direction of the applied shear stress [ 52 ]. This σ h  can offset part of the applied shear stress, which indirectly increases the critical stress required to activate the dislocation source, and manifests as σ h  strengthening [ 53 ]. The σ h  strengthening and hardening are the collective result of interactions between back stress and forward stress [ 54 ]. The development of back stress in ferrite and forward stress in bainite can be understood in  Fig. 9 (g). As shown in  Fig. 9 (g), GNDs are emitted from a Frank-Read (F–R) dislocation source in the ferrite [ 55 ]. Assuming the F–R source can be activated at a critical shear stress of τ 0 , there are several GNDs emitted at applied shear stress τ a  (τ a  > τ 0 ), which are piled up against the interface [ 56 ]. The stresses are concentrated at the interface on the ferrite side, and on the bainite side, there must be stress to balance it. This stress on the bainite side should promote the strain localization of the bainite. That is, the stress on the bainite side is the same as the driving effect of the applied stress on the dislocation slip. Therefore, the stress in the bainite induced by the GNDs pile up in the ferrite is named the forward stress [ 47 ]. At the F/B interface, the back stress and forward stress are the same in their magnitude but opposite in their directions. The interaction between back stress and forward stress is not a zero-sum game [ 54 ]. They cancel each other at the F/B interface because they have the same magnitude but opposite directions. However, they have different profiles as a function of distance away from the F/B interface. This difference gives rise to the observed σ h  strengthening and hardening of dual-phase steel.

The σ h  strengthening and hardening from the production of GNDs are the main reasons for the excellent strain hardening ability and plasticity of the dual-phase structure [ 57 ]. As a whole, F–R sources are first activated in ferrite, followed by dislocation entanglement and accumulation, the strain difference between ferrite and bainite is reduced, and strain localization occurs at the F/B interface [ 58 ]. This leads to the continuous generation of GNDs, which can give rise to σ h . These GNDs, located mainly near the phase boundary, are used to coordinate the incompatibility of ferrite and bainite deformation. With the increase of tensile LUR strain, for one thing, less and less room is left for ferrite to further accommodate more dislocations, which leads to hardly any mobile dislocations upon yielding when reloading, as evidenced by the enhanced σ 0.2  ( Fig. 6 (d)) [ 2 ]. For another, more GNDs, if possible, will be generated near the heterostructure interface to achieve sustainable tensile plasticity of dual-phase steel. Hence, the σ h  makes the heterostructure reasonably modify the excellent strength and the plastic deformation ability as tensile LUR strain increases. Whereafter, in the failure process of dual-phase steel, the GNDs inhibit the crack propagation, while the σ h  reduces the driving force of dislocation slip and makes it difficult for the dislocation source to start, which in turn acts on the crack propagation. The strain localization at the F/B interface maintained the tensile plasticity of the heterogeneous structure during the tensile process, while microcracks and micropores formed near the interface after the F/B interface gradually hardened, and then the cracks begin to initiate at the interface ( Fig. 7 ). The final fracture of F/B dual-phase structure tends to transiter from ductile fracture to brittle fracture ( Fig. 8 (k)).

sections.heading: Conclusions
paragraphs: Herein, the X80 steel provides an ideal opportunity to reveal hetero-deformation, specifically, the HDI stress (σ h ) induced prominent hardening. The hysteresis loop appears during the design of tensile load-unload-reload (LUR), indicative of the operation of σ h  related to the production of geometrically necessary dislocations (GNDs). In addition, the descent of strain hardening rate is a sign of insufficient mobile dislocations. The σ h  induced strain localization and hardening, which ameliorates the strength and tensile plasticity of the dual-phase steel. The persistent presence of both hysteresis loops and a small difference in yield is visible during tensile LUR. It is further demonstrated that the σ h  induced hardening accounts for global strain hardening. The generated σ h  by the accumulation of GNDs inhibits the dislocation motion, the hardening behavior of heterostructure from ferrite hardening to F/B interfacial hardening. Hence, strain localization and hardening induced by σ h  are proposed to improve the tensile deformation incompatibility of the dual-phase steel. Wherein, a vast plastic mismatch between two phases serves as the microstructural origin of σ h . In response to dual-phase structure tensile plasticity, the GNDs have to be formed to accommodate deformation incompatibility. Ultimately, we identify that the fracture failure of dual-phase steel structure tends to transition from initial ductile fracture to brittle fracture.
